title: Spiders Step in Their Own Glue 100s of Times. Why? 🕷️
description:
Why don't spiders get stuck in their own webs? Only the spiral threads of an orb web carry glue, web spiders grip single threads with a third claw, and branched hairs plus a non-stick coating on their legs make glue droplets slide off.

topic: Why don't spiders get stuck in their own webs?
script: Spider glue almost never lets a fly go. So why do you never see the spider stuck? Secret one: most of the web isn't sticky. The spokes are dry silk. Only the spiral has beads of glue, so the spider walks the spokes. Secret two: its feet. Web spiders have three claws per foot. Insects get two. The extra claw hooks a single thread, like a tiny hand. But here's the wild part. Building one web, a spider touches its own glue hundreds of times. Its legs are covered in branched hairs, so the glue slides along them and drips off. Scientists washed spider legs, and they stuck more. So there's a non-stick coating, too. A fly hits lots of glue at once. The spider barely touches a drop. So which trick would you steal: the claws, the hairs, or the coating?
key_facts: Orb webs: the radial spokes are dry silk, only the spiral carries glue droplets (How It Works; Burke Museum: webs have many non-sticky threads)
Web-building spiders have a third tarsal claw that grips single threads; insects have at most two (Burke Museum)
Briceno & Eberhard 2012 (Naturwissenschaften, STRI/Univ. of Costa Rica): orb weavers touch their sticky silk hundreds to thousands of times while building one web
Branched hairs on the legs let glue droplets slide along and drip off; washing legs with hexane made them stick more, showing a non-stick coating (Smithsonian / phys.org)
Spiders tiptoe around the glue and touch few droplets, while a fly hits many at once (Burke Museum, Vollrath & Tillinghast 1992)
